en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
I shall speak, having extracted [this] from various teachers, regarding the Pāli of the Cāṇakya-nīti.
This compendium of royal policy,
this treatise containing all seeds,
is the *Cāṇakya-sārasaṅgaha*.
I shall proclaim the root-sūtra as it was spoken by Cāṇakya;
by the mere understanding of which—
The fool becomes wise;
there is never any equality between one who has transcended and a mere human being.
A king is honored in his own country;
a wise man is honored everywhere.
All virtues belong to the learned.
For faults belong solely to the deluded;
therefore, among thousands of deluded ones,
a single wise person excels.
As toward one's own mother, so toward the wives of others;
as toward one's own kinsmen, so toward the wives of others;
as toward oneself, so toward all living beings.
The wise person sees this:
What is the use of a noble lineage for a man who is devoid of virtue?
Even one who is unlearned, if he knows the scriptures,
is honored even by the deities;
yet those endowed with beauty and youth [are not].
Those born of a noble lineage do not shine if they are devoid of knowledge,
like *kiṃsuka* trees stripped of their bark.
The moon is the ornament of the stars,
the husband is the ornament of women,
and the king is the ornament of the earth.
Knowledge is the ornament of all.
A mother who is an enemy and a father who is a foe is he by whom a fool has not been supported.
He does not shine in the midst of the assembly,
like a crane in the midst of swans.
Better is one virtuous son.
Nor even by hundreds of fools;
a single moon dispels the darkness,
not even by the hosts of stars.
One should pamper [the child] for five years,
strike him for ten years;
but when he has reached his sixteenth year, [one should treat him as an adult].
One should treat a son like a friend.
There are many faults in pampering him,
but many virtues in disciplining him.
Therefore, one should not pamper either a son or a pupil;
rather, one should encourage them with even a single well-spoken word.
With its blossoming fragrance,
it perfumes the entire forest,
just as a well-cooked meal perfumes a household.
Even by the fire from a single hollow tree,
the entire forest is consumed.
Like a family with a foolish son,
he shines from afar though deluded,
draped in hanging garments.
The fool shines as long as he says nothing;
once he speaks, his lack of wisdom is revealed.
Having grasped the deathless, the wise man shines.
Even from one who is not dear may come gold;
even from a lowly person may come the highest knowledge;
even from a woman of poor birth may come the jewel of a wife.
During festivals and calamities,
during famine and civil strife,
at the king’s gate and in the cemetery—
He who stands with all his kinsmen—
him who destroys what must be done in one's absence,
yet speaks kindly when face to face;
One should avoid such a friend as a jar of poison with milk on its surface;
for one who [associates with] a friend who has once turned wicked—
Again he desires to join together;
he grasps it completely,
just as a mother does her child in the womb.
One should not trust the untrustworthy,
nor should one trust even a friend;
for a friend may at some time become angry.
One should disclose all faults.
One should know one's servants in their duties,
and one's kinsmen in times of misfortune.
A friend at the time of need,
a wife when wealth has failed, and one who is held fast by a prior favor—
these are difficult to find.
One should extract an enemy by means of an enemy,
just as one extracts a thorn from the foot with another thorn.
No one is anyone's friend,
nor is anyone anyone's enemy;
for it is by reason that one is known.
Friends and likewise enemies,
the wicked person and the sweet-talker—
none of these are grounds for trust.
Honey stays upon the tip of the tongue,
but in the heart is the halāhala poison.
A wicked person should be avoided.
Even though he is adorned with knowledge,
what fear does a snake not produce,
even when decorated with a jewel?
A snake is cruel, a rogue is cruel;
a rogue is more cruel than a snake.
A snake can be charmed with a mantra, but a rogue cannot be lived with.
By what is a wicked person restrained?
By nails, by rivers, by horned beasts,
and by those who carry weapons in their hands.
Trust should never be placed in women or in royal families.
An elephant [is no match] for a thousand elephants.
A horse is tamed by the hand of the trainer;
a horned beast by the hand of ten;
but a wicked person is difficult to tame even by the giving up of one's position.
One should guard wealth for the sake of misfortune,
guard one's wife even at the cost of wealth,
and always guard oneself.
Through wives and through wealth,
[one commits] adultery with another's wife,
theft of another's property, and slander of another.
One should avoid jesting in the presence of elders and abandon fickleness;
one may sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family.
For the sake of a village, one may abandon a family;
for the sake of a village, one may abandon a district;
but for the sake of oneself, one may abandon the entire earth.
The wise man moves with one foot and stands with one;
he does not step forward without having scrutinized the ground ahead.
One should abandon former associations.
The greedy man may win wealth,
and the stubborn man may win honor through his actions.
One follows the whims of a deluded person,
and likewise those of a wise one;
this leads to the destruction of one's welfare and brings mental anguish.
One who possesses wisdom should not disclose their misdeeds,
nor their deceits, nor their limits.
In the management of wealth and grain,
likewise in the sciences and arts,
in food and in worldly transactions,
One should always be free from shame.
A wealthy man, a physician, a king, a river, and fifthly, a physician.
One should not make one's dwelling where these five are not found:
where there is no respect for one's country.
Where there is no joy, nor kinsmen,
nor any attainment of knowledge— one should avoid that place.
One should not reveal with speech an action conceived by the mind;
for one who acts on what is characterized by another [is lost].
Since success is not achieved through a bad country, a wrong livelihood,
a bad wife, or likewise a bad river.
A wise person should avoid bad food and bad drink;
likewise, one should avoid remaining debt and the residue of what was previously consumed.
And likewise, if there remains a portion of the disease,
it will increase again;
therefore, one should not leave any remainder.
Worry is the fever of human beings;
the heat of the sun is the fever of clothes;
lack of beauty is the fever of women.
For horses, sexual union is old age.
He who has a son living at home,
as well as a wife and a brother-in-law—
Even in the absence of wealth, there is great contentment;
that is a state of heaven upon this earth.
A wicked wife and a deceitful friend—
One who gives food is a giver of life;
even living in a house full of snakes,
death is certain for him, there is no doubt.
He in whose house there is no mother,
nor even a wife who speaks kindly,
should go to the forest.
Just as it is for kings, so it is for this house:
the father is a debtor and an enemy,
and the mother is unchaste.
A beautiful wife is an enemy;
an unwise son is an enemy.
The song of cuckoos is their bane.
Faithfulness is the beauty of women;
knowledge is the beauty of the ugly;
forbearance is the beauty of ascetics.
Ignorance is an empty life;
the quarters are empty and without kin;
a home bereft of children is empty.
Poverty is entirely empty [of intrinsic nature];
poverty arises from the fault of lineage and from the fault of karma.
Insanity arises from the fault of the mother;
delusion from the fault of the father.
Fire is the teacher for the twice-born and others.
The brahmin is the teacher of the castes;
the husband alone is the teacher of women;
and the guest is the teacher of all.
Lanka was destroyed by excessive pride;
the Kauravas by excessive arrogance;
and the ox by excessive giving.
Everything has been completely grasped.
But an ornament without its base,
and food without its vessel— these are of no use.
A woman without a husband, life without knowledge,
food without the power of digestion.
For one whose passion for women is supreme,
and whose wealth is spent on the passion for giving,
the fruit of asceticism will not be seen.
A wife has the purpose of bearing children;
a son has the purpose of providing alms;
a friend has the purpose of promoting one's welfare.
Wealth serves every purpose.
Natural speech is hard to find;
a son who brings security is hard to find.
A wife who is one's equal is hard to find;
a dear friend is also hard to find.
Just as a diamond is rare on every mountain, so too are these things rare.
Not every elephant trumpets like a rutting bull;
indeed, the virtuous are not found everywhere;
nor does sandalwood grow in every forest.
One who is without grief, free from debt, and wise;
one who is without grief and a kinsman of the learned;
a woman who is without grief and not a widow.
Established in the state of a putta,
the ignorant man grieves;
he grieves for sexual union that is not his own.
Seeing that people are without sustenance,
one should grieve for the sorrow of a kingdom without a king,
which has utterly perished along with its clans.
Maintaining friendship with the wise and forming equal bonds with kinsmen—
one who acts thus shall not come to ruin.
Livelihood depends on others,
dwelling is without expectation,
and effort is devoid of wealth.
When all things are in a state of poverty, where can the doer find the Dhamma?
Where can the wicked person find forbearance?
Whence can there be affection for a courtesan,
whence truth for one who lusts?
Whence can there be pride in one who is sent away?
Whence can there be happiness for one who is agitated?
Whence can there be mindfulness for one who is slothful?
And whence can there be loving-kindness for a wicked person?
The king is the strength of the weak;
weeping is the strength of fools;
silence is the strength of the bewildered.
The strength of thieves is their falsehood.
He who abandons what is stable and pursues what is unstable—
His certainties perish,
and that which is uncertain has already perished.
White flesh, women, and the aged—
Milk from a young cow, fresh curd,
sexual intercourse at dawn, and sleep during the day—
these six things, when fresh, are life-destroying.
Fresh meat and new rice,
fools and women, food with milk, ghee,
and warm water— these are the eight things that are difficult to obtain.
There are six [animals] that provide meat while alive:
one from the lion, one from the crane,
six from dogs, and three from the donkey.
One should learn four things from a crow and four even from a cock;
whether it be much or little that needs to be done.
The one who wishes to act must do so with restraint;
this single point has been illustrated by the lion.
All the faculties are restrained;
the man has fallen like Baka,
having encountered the right time and place.
May he accomplish all his tasks.
May he eat much, be easily satisfied,
have a good appetite, and possess quick intelligence.
One who eats moderately and is brave—
these six qualities of a good dog should be known.
It carries its burden without resting.
He does not feel cold or heat;
being thus constantly contented—
these three things, O camels, you should train yourselves in.
The practice of secret sexual intercourse,
gathering together from time to time,
heedfulness, and lack of indolence.
One should learn four things from crows:
fighting, rising early in the morning,
eating together with kinsmen, and [storing] food.
One should protect one who has fallen into calamity;
one should learn four things from a cock;
a burden of a hundred million is not too heavy for those who are capable.
Who is far away? One who is industrious.
What is a foreign land for those possessed of knowledge?
Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly?
Lack of restraint over the sense faculties is said to be the path to fear;
their conquest is the way to true attainment.
By that one goes to a new birth.
There is no kinsman equal to knowledge,
and no enemy equal to disease.
Neither is affection equal to that of a mother,
nor are the gods a superior power.
The earth is bounded by the oceans.
A house is enclosed by a wall;
countries are enclosed by kings;
women are enclosed by their conduct.
A woman is like a water-jar;
a man is like a glowing ember.
Therefore, [one should avoid] both the jar and the fire.
The wise person should set aside a portion:
food is twofold [the cause] of sloth,
while wisdom is fourfold [the antidote].
One quality is the exertion,
and desire is considered to have eight qualities.
One should praise food that has been digested.
A wife whose youth has passed,
a hero returned from battle,
and grain that has come home.
The twice-born are ruined by discontent,
while kings are ruined by contentment;
the courtesan is ruined by modesty.
Shameless women and noble ladies;
a king fallen from his throne and a fool who is wise.
Having acquired wealth through improper means,
a person regards others as mere straw; yet even a man who has killed a brahmin is worthy of honor [if he has attained such wealth].
Even one who possesses vast wealth and a lineage equal to the moon is treated with contempt if he is destitute.
But books, as long as they exist,
and wealth that has passed into the hands of others,
when the time for action has arisen—
There is no fear for the ignorant, nor is there wealth for them.
Wind is the fear of trees;
cold is the fear of lotuses.
Among mountains, there is fear of the thunderbolt;
among the virtuous, there is fear of the wicked.
But when wisdom is applied, [there is no fear].
A king possesses three qualities:
renown, residence in heaven,
and an abundant influx of wealth.
When one who is deluded is being appointed [to office],
there are three faults for the kshatriya:
infamy, loss of wealth, and destruction.
Likewise, there is going to hell,
through many who are deluded and crowded together,
living like one animal after another.
All virtues are obscured,
like the sun by clouds;
for one whose field is on the riverbank, [the harvest is lost].
Even a wife may be dear to others;
there is no discipline for a son—
death is indeed certain.
The impossible and the inexplicable are seen even before one's very eyes:
a stone floats upon the water.
The monkey sings a song:
"May there always be plenty for the farmers,
and may there always be happiness and freedom from disease."
The house of one whose wife is dear to her husband is always leaking;
it is a source of ruin through negligence.
Beggary leads to the destruction of intelligence;
begging leads to the loss of honor;
and eating [at others' houses] leads to the ruin of one's family.
The great banyan tree should be cultivated,
for it is endowed with both fruit and shade; even if there is no fruit, O gods, [the shade remains].
Who can ward off the shadow?
In the first case, knowledge was lost;
in the second, wealth was lost.
In the third [life] the merit is exhausted;
what will it do in the fourth?
And those who speak on the riverbank—
Wealth that has passed into the hands of others,
and whatever duty is performed for one whose sphere of activity is women— all that becomes fruitless.
Having encountered a bad neighbor, whence can there be an accumulation of wealth?
Having encountered a bad son, whence can there be funeral offerings?
Having obtained a bad wife in the home, whence can there be happiness?
For one who burns his own dwelling, whence can there be fame?
It is like well-water, the shade of a banyan tree,
a woman, a heap of chaff, and a shelter for a crow.
In the cold season there is warmth,
and in the hot season there is coolness;
and at night, the walking-path is like poison.
Poison is a king’s lack of loyalty;
poison is a woman attached to another;
poison is a disease that has been neglected.
Ill-studied knowledge is poison;
food that is undigested is poison;
for the poor man, social gathering is poison.
A young woman is poison to an old man;
a path is destroyed by hatred;
women are defeated when they fall.
A field with no seeds is ruined;
a lord with faults in his food is ruined;
a faithful person without learning is ruined.
A sacrifice without a priest is ruined;
a beautiful woman who is barren is ruined;
an army without a leader is ruined.
Knowing the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
devoted to recitation and burnt offerings,
and intent on uttering words of blessing—
This is the king’s chaplain,
endowed with noble birth, virtue, and good qualities, and devoted to all that is righteous.
The practice of the messenger and so forth,
and the practice of the dharma and so forth, are prescribed; the practice of the fathom-high enclosure (āyubbedaka) is likewise established.
Pleasing to behold to all,
endowed with the virtues of noble conduct—
this is the Vajja that is prescribed.
Having grasped the meaning once,
with a light hand and mastery over syllables,
he surveys the entire body of treatises.
Pakaṭṭha was the name of a scribe;
he knew the seven principles of ethics in their entirety and was equal to Pūjita in matters of transport.
Endowed with the qualities of a brave hero,
he is appointed as the commander-in-chief;
he is pure, eloquent, and possessed of keen wisdom.
One who observes the minds of others,
who is wise, and who speaks according to the truth—
such a person is appointed as a messenger.
Puttanatta was endowed with virtues,
another teacher was a baker,
and there were also Sūra and Kathina.
He is called a cook: one who understands the truth of gestures and appearances,
who is strong and pleasing to behold.
He who is always diligent and skillful is called a "counter-measure.
For one who lacks wisdom themselves—
What can a sword do for him?
What can a mirror do for one who is deprived of eyes?
What can those who speak do where no one listens?
In a region of naked beggars, what can they achieve?
What will the king do?
